title: Dytective gamified online dyslexia screener reaches 80.6% recall on 3,644 Spanish-speaking children (PLoS ONE 2020); a 2026 re-analysis finds a demographic confound
summary: Rello et al.'s random-forest screener, tested on 3,644 children from 113 organizations in five countries, 79.8% accuracy; the tool has been used over 200,000 times. A 2026 paper reports confounding.
account: Luz Rello (IE University, Madrid), Baeza-Yates, Ali, Bigham and Serra published in PLoS ONE (2 December 2020) a web-based gamified test of 32 linguistic exercises. Its performance measures feed a random-forest classifier with 200 trees. The study enrolled 3,644 participants aged 7–17, 392 with a professional dyslexia diagnosis, recruited through 113 organizations in Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Spain and the USA. They were 60 primary and secondary schools, 22 specialized dyslexia centers, 18 non-profits and 3 universities. The classifier reached 79.8% accuracy with 80.6% recall and 79.3% precision for the dyslexia class. A tablet validation with 1,395 participants aged 12–17 gave 78.1% recall and 76.2% precision. The authors state that an online Spanish screening tool based on their methods had already been used by more than 200,000 people. They disclose a patent application (US 15/493,060, Rello and Ballesteros). Sudha and Murali (Frontiers in Digital Health, 23 September 2026) re-analyzed the same 3,644-participant dataset. They report that dyslexia prevalence in the dataset differs 4.7-fold by native-language status. Four demographic columns alone reach AUC 0.724 against 0.744 for all 192 task metrics. Including them yields a twelve-fold disparity in false-positive rate between language groups. The date observed is the PLoS ONE publication date.
purpose: Dytective was designed to screen children for dyslexia risk cheaply online. The accuracy figures and usage are that purpose.
system: Dytective online gamified dyslexia screening test with a random-forest classifier
model_version: Weka 3.8.3 implementation with 200 trees and unlimited height
developer: Luz Rello and co-authors (IE University, Northeastern, University of Washington, Carnegie Mellon, University of Barcelona), per the paper's author list
deployer: Schools, dyslexia centers and non-profits in Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Spain and the USA (study participants); public online use in Spanish-speaking countries

ratings.reason: No individually attributable outcome: the sources report classifier accuracy (80.6% recall) and aggregate use (over 200,000 people), not what followed a screening result.
No outcome documented for the 60 participating schools or the other organizations beyond supplying participants.

ai_role.statement: The random-forest classifier is the screening decision. The 2026 re-analysis shows that demographic variables alone reach nearly the same AUC in this dataset and that false-positive rates differ twelve-fold between language groups. So the measured accuracy may partly reflect sample composition.

headline: Dytective online dyslexia screener reaches 80.6% recall

later.note: An independent re-analysis of the same dataset reported that four demographic columns alone nearly match the 192 task metrics' discrimination and that including them yields a twelve-fold false-positive disparity between language groups, undercutting the screener's reported performance.
later.quote: A subgroup audit shows that dyslexia prevalence in this dataset differs 4.7-fold by native-language status, that four demographic columns alone reach AUC 0.724 against 0.744 for all 192 task metrics, and that including them yields a twelve-fold disparity in false-positive rate between language groups.
